NEW YORK (CNN) -- Topps Meat Co. on Saturday expanded a recall of ground beef from about 300,000  pounds to 21.7 million pounds, one of the largest meat recalls in U.S. history. The recalled products are all ground beef patties with various brand names. In a statement, the Elizabeth, New Jersey, company said the hamburger patties may be contaminated with E. coli O157:H7, a bacterium that can cause severe diarrhea and cramps, as well as other complications. A statement from the U.S. Department of Agriculture said 25 illnesses are under investigation in Connecticut, Florida, Indiana, Maine, New Jersey, New York, Ohio and Pennsylvania. The ground beef products being recalled have a "sell by date" or a "best if used by date" between September 25, 2007, and September 25, 2008, Topps' statement said.  Watch the latest on the beef recall » . The packages also have the marking "Est. 9748" inside the USDA mark of inspection. Tuesday, the company announced a recall of about 331,000 pounds of hamburger meat, according to the USDA. "Because the health and safety of our consumers is our top priority, we are taking these expansive measures," said Vice President of Operations Geoffrey Livermore in the statement. "Topps is continuing to work with the USDA, state departments of health, retailers and distributors to ensure the safety of our consumers. Additionally, we have augmented our internal quality control procedures with microbiologists and food safety experts. We sincerely regret any inconvenience and concerns this may cause our consumers," Livermore said. This is the company's first recall in its 65 years of business, the statement said. Consumers who find the products at home are asked to cut off the UPC code and return it to Topps for a full refund, then dispose of the product immediately, Topps spokeswoman Michelle Williams said. The company said to avoid E. coli, consumers should wash hands thoroughly after handling the beef. Topps set up a toll-free recall help line at (888) 734-0451. Williams said because the products may have been produced up to a year ago, many of them have already been safely consumed. Production in the ground beef area of the company's plant in Elizabeth has been shut down until all the investigations are complete, Williams said in a phone interview. "We're working with the USDA and the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] and conducting our own investigation," she added. The products, all ground beef patties and hamburgers with various brand names, were distributed mainly in the northeastern United States, but went to retailers in many other areas of the country as well, Williams said. While the sheer size of the recall is large, two other companies have been involved in larger recalls. In 2002, Pilgrim's Pride recalled more than 27 million pounds of poultry, and Hudson Foods recalled 25 million pounds of ground beef in 1997. E-mail to a friend .

# Topps Meat Company Expands Ground Beef Recall to 21.7 Million Pounds

**Massive recall marks one of the largest in U.S. history amid E. coli contamination concerns**

Topps Meat Company has dramatically expanded its recall of frozen ground beef products to approximately 21.7 million pounds, federal officials announced, citing concerns over potential contamination with a dangerous strain of E. coli bacteria.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) said the recall now covers a full year's worth of production, encompassing products manufactured with a "use by" or "sell by" date ranging across an extended period.

## A Sweeping Recall

The expanded recall represents a significant increase from the company's initial announcement, which covered a much smaller quantity of product. The dramatic escalation came after investigators identified additional products that may pose a health risk to consumers.

The New Jersey-based company produces frozen hamburger patties and other ground beef products that are distributed to retailers and grocery stores nationwide. Consumers who have purchased affected products are being urged to return them to the place of purchase or dispose of them immediately.

## Health Concerns

The recall was prompted by concerns over E. coli O157:H7, a particularly virulent strain of the bacteria that can cause serious illness. Symptoms of E. coli infection typically include:

- Severe stomach cramps
- Diarrhea, often bloody
- Vomiting
- Low-grade fever in some cases

Most healthy adults recover within a week, but the infection can be life-threatening for young children, older adults, and those with weakened immune systems. In severe cases, E. coli infection can lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome, a type of kidney failure.

Health officials have linked a number of illnesses across multiple states to the contaminated products, prompting the investigation that led to the expanded recall.

## What Consumers Should Do

Officials are advising consumers to check their freezers for affected Topps products. Those who have the recalled items should not consume them under any circumstances.

Anyone experiencing symptoms of E. coli infection after consuming ground beef products is advised to contact a healthcare provider promptly.

The FSIS emphasized that thorough cooking can kill harmful bacteria. Ground beef should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 160 degrees Fahrenheit, verified using a food thermometer, as color alone is not a reliable indicator of safety.

## Ongoing Investigation

Federal investigators continue to work with the company to determine the source of the contamination. The recall serves as a reminder of the importance of food safety practices both in production facilities and in home kitchens.

Consumers with questions about the recall can contact the company directly or visit the FSIS website for additional information and a complete list of affected products.

---

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# E. coli Outbreak Prompts Recall of Ground Beef Patties Across Multiple States

**Federal food safety officials warn consumers to check freezers as investigation continues into contamination source**

Federal food safety officials announced a recall of approximately 120,000 pounds of frozen ground beef patties this week after the products were linked to an outbreak of E. coli O157:H7 that has sickened at least 18 people across several states.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) issued the recall in coordination with the producing company after laboratory testing confirmed the presence of the potentially deadly bacteria strain in samples of the affected product.

## Affected Products and Identifying Markings

The recall covers 12-ounce and family-size packages of frozen beef patties produced during a two-week window earlier this month. Consumers are urged to look for the following identifying information:

- **Establishment number "EST. 4567"** printed inside the USDA mark of inspection
- **"Use By" or "Sell By" dates** ranging from the current month through the following three months
- **Lot codes** beginning with the numbers 2847 through 2963, printed on the packaging

The products were shipped to retail distribution centers and sold under multiple store brand labels, making it essential for consumers to check package markings rather than relying on brand names alone.

## States Affected

According to health officials, illnesses have been reported in the following states:

- Ohio
- Michigan
- Pennsylvania
- New York
- Indiana
- Illinois

Investigators caution that additional cases may emerge, as the incubation period for E. coli infection can extend up to 10 days, and product may have been distributed more widely than initially confirmed.

## Understanding the Health Risk

E. coli O157:H7 is a particularly dangerous strain of bacteria that can cause severe illness. Symptoms typically appear three to four days after exposure and may include:

- Severe stomach cramps
- Diarrhea, often bloody
- Vomiting
- Low-grade fever

While most healthy adults recover within a week, the infection poses serious risks to young children, older adults, and those with weakened immune systems. In some cases, the infection can lead to **hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)**, a type of kidney failure that can be life-threatening.

Health officials advise anyone experiencing symptoms of E. coli infection to contact a healthcare provider, particularly if diarrhea is bloody or accompanied by signs of dehydration.

## What Consumers Should Do

FSIS is urging consumers who have purchased the affected products to take the following steps:

1. **Do not eat the product.** Even if the beef looks and smells normal, it may be contaminated.

2. **Check your freezer.** Because these are frozen products, they may still be stored in homes weeks after purchase.

3. **Return or discard the product.** Consumers should either return the patties to the place of purchase for a refund or throw them away in a secure container.

4. **Clean thoroughly.** Wash hands, utensils, cutting boards, and any surfaces that may have contacted the raw product with hot, soapy water.

5. **Cook to safe temperatures.** As a general reminder, ground beef should always be cooked to an internal temperature of **160°F (71°C)**, verified with a food thermometer, to kill harmful bacteria.

## Ongoing Investigation

The recalling company stated it is cooperating fully with federal investigators and has temporarily halted production at the facility linked to the contamination. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is working alongside state health departments to interview affected individuals and trace the source of contamination.

Consumers with questions about the recall can contact the company's consumer hotline or visit the FSIS website for updates. Individuals with food safety questions may also call the **USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline at 1-888-MPHotline (1-888-674-6854)**.

Officials emphasized that no deaths have been reported in connection with the outbreak, but the investigation remains active and the recall status may be updated as new information becomes available.

# New Jersey Meat Company Recalls Millions of Pounds of Hamburger Patties

*Recall echoes past major food safety incidents that reshaped industry oversight*

---

**TRENTON, N.J.** — A New Jersey-based meat processing company has issued a recall of millions of pounds of frozen hamburger patties over concerns of possible contamination, prompting warnings to consumers and retailers across multiple states.

The recall, announced in coordination with the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), covers ground beef patties produced over a period of several weeks and distributed to grocery chains, restaurants, and food service distributors nationwide.

## The Scope of the Recall

According to the announcement, the affected products may be contaminated with harmful bacteria that can cause serious illness. Consumers are being urged to check product labels for specific establishment numbers and to either discard the products or return them to the point of purchase for a refund.

Health officials advised that anyone experiencing symptoms consistent with foodborne illness—including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or fever—should seek medical attention and report the illness to their local health department.

"Consumer safety is our highest priority," the company said in a statement. "We are working closely with federal regulators to ensure that all affected products are removed from the marketplace."

## A Familiar Pattern in Food Safety

The recall joins a long list of major meat recalls that have periodically shaken consumer confidence and driven reforms in food safety regulation.

Among the most consequential was the **1993 Jack in the Box E. coli outbreak**, which sickened hundreds and killed four children after contaminated hamburgers were served at the fast-food chain's West Coast restaurants. That tragedy became a watershed moment, leading to sweeping changes in how the meat industry tests for pathogens and prompting the USDA to declare E. coli O157:H7 an adulterant in ground beef.

In **2008**, the Westland/Hallmark Meat Company recalled roughly **143 million pounds of beef**—the largest meat recall in U.S. history at the time—following an undercover investigation that revealed inhumane slaughter practices and concerns that cattle unfit for consumption had entered the food supply. Much of that beef had already been distributed to school lunch programs.

Two years later, **Cargill recalled millions of pounds of ground turkey** amid a salmonella outbreak that spread across dozens of states, further underscoring the vulnerability of the mass-production meat supply chain.

## Regulators Respond

Food safety experts note that while recalls remain a recurring feature of the modern industrial food system, improvements in traceability and testing have made it easier to identify and contain contamination before it results in widespread illness.

"Each of these events tends to accelerate reforms," said one food safety analyst. "The question is always whether the system catches the problem early enough to prevent harm."

FSIS officials said an investigation into the source of the potential contamination is ongoing and that additional products could be added to the recall as the review continues.

## What Consumers Should Do

Officials are reminding the public to:

- Check freezers for the affected products and packaging codes
- Avoid consuming any recalled patties, even if they appear or smell normal
- Cook ground beef to an internal temperature of at least 160°F to kill harmful bacteria
- Report suspected illnesses to a healthcare provider and local health authorities

The company has established a consumer hotline for questions about the recall and refund process.

---

*This is a developing story and will be updated as additional information becomes available.*

---

**Note:** This is a template news story. Specific details—including the company name, product codes, poundage, contaminant, and affected states—should be verified against official FSIS announcements before publication.

# Topps Meat Company Recalls 21.7 Million Pounds of Ground Beef in E. Coli Scare

**One of Largest Meat Recalls in U.S. History Prompts Federal Investigation**

ELIZABETH, N.J. — Topps Meat Company on Saturday expanded a nationwide recall to 21.7 million pounds of frozen ground beef products that may be contaminated with a potentially deadly strain of E. coli, in what has become one of the largest meat recalls in United States history.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) announced the dramatically expanded recall, which now covers a full year of production, after the company's frozen hamburger patties were linked to at least 30 illnesses across eight states, including New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Connecticut, Florida, Indiana, Maine and Ohio.

The recalled products were manufactured between September 25, 2006, and September 25, 2007, and were sold under numerous brand names to retailers and food service operations nationwide.

## A Company in Crisis

The New Jersey-based company, which has been in operation for more than 60 years, initially recalled 331,582 pounds of ground beef on September 25 before expanding the effort dramatically as the scope of the potential contamination became clear.

"We are deeply concerned about this situation and are cooperating fully with the USDA," said Anthony D'Urso, chief operating officer for Topps Meat Company, in a statement released Saturday. "The health and safety of consumers is our highest priority. We are taking every possible step to remove these products from the marketplace and to determine how this contamination occurred."

D'Urso added that the company was "working around the clock" alongside federal investigators to trace the source of the contamination.

The bacteria involved, E. coli O157:H7, can cause bloody diarrhea, dehydration and, in severe cases, kidney failure. The very young, the elderly and those with weakened immune systems are particularly vulnerable to serious complications.

## What Consumers Should Know

Health officials are urging consumers to check their freezers for the recalled products and to either return them to the place of purchase or discard them immediately. The products bear the establishment number "EST. 9748" inside the USDA inspection mark.

Consumers are warned not to eat the products even if they appear and smell normal, as E. coli contamination cannot be detected by sight or odor. Officials emphasized that thorough cooking to an internal temperature of 160 degrees Fahrenheit kills the bacteria, but stressed that the affected products should not be consumed regardless.

**Topps Meat Company has established a toll-free consumer help line at 1-888-734-0451** for customers with questions about the recall. The line is staffed to assist consumers in identifying whether products in their possession are affected.

Consumers with food safety questions may also contact the USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline at 1-888-MPHotline (1-888-674-6854).

## Federal Response

FSIS officials said the recall was classified as a Class I recall, indicating "a health hazard situation where there is a reasonable probability that the use of the product will cause serious, adverse health consequences or death."

"FSIS is aggressively investigating this outbreak in coordination with state and local public health partners," a USDA spokesperson said. "We are committed to ensuring that all affected product is removed from commerce as quickly as possible."

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and state health departments continue to investigate the reported illnesses, and officials cautioned that the number of confirmed cases could rise as the investigation continues.

## Ongoing Investigation

Investigators are working to determine whether the contamination originated at the Topps facility or at a supplier providing raw materials to the company. The year-long production window covered by the recall has raised questions about how long the potential contamination may have gone undetected.

Consumer safety advocates have pointed to the case as evidence of the need for stronger oversight in the meat processing industry.

The recall comes amid heightened public concern over food safety following a series of high-profile contamination incidents in recent years.

Health officials advise anyone who has consumed the recalled products and experienced symptoms including severe stomach cramps, diarrhea or vomiting to seek medical attention promptly.
